generatedProse.concept-context: Across disciplines, the value of a degree is easy to undersell as a grade. A degree builds human capital in the knowledge and skills of a field, and social capital through the networks you form with peers, tutors and placements. It builds cultural capital in how your field argues and behaves, and identity capital as you decide what kind of professional you are becoming. It builds psychological capital too, through the resilience the work itself demands. Seeing all five is what turns a transcript into a case you can actually make.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who reach the end of the same degree with similar marks, and are each asked in an interview what they have gained.

{{learner-a}} talks only about modules passed and the final grade. It is accurate, but it is all human capital, and only the paper kind. The panel learns what {{learner-a}} studied, not what {{learner-a}} can offer an organisation, who they can work with, or how they handle setbacks.

{{learner-b}} gives the grade, then adds more: a project that built a network of collaborators, a placement that showed how the field actually works, and a demanding piece of work that proved real resilience. {{learner-b}} is describing human, social, cultural and psychological capital together, with a clear sense of the professional they are becoming.

Both earned the degree. Only {{learner-b}} could evaluate it across the five forms, and so made the stronger case.
generatedProse.summary: Graduate capital reframes success as the resources a degree builds, not marks alone. Tomlinson's framework names five forms: human, social, cultural, identity and psychological capital. You can now explain why this reframes success beyond a grade, tell the five forms apart, and evaluate which ones your own degree is building and which you are neglecting.

check.body: A student describes the professional networks and relationships they have built during their degree. Which form of graduate capital is this?

feedback.correct: That's right. Networks and relationships are social capital.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Which form names the connections you build with other people?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Networks and relationships are social capital. Human capital is skills and knowledge, cultural capital is knowing how the field works, and psychological capital is resilience.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
